slides.title: First, a confession
slides.caption: Unrelated. A good boy in a DEV DOG hoodie who commits with "woof". That is the whole joke. Moving on.

box.content:
I have deployed code on a Friday afternoon. I have also spent that weekend undoing it while a client called every two hours.

I say this so we start honest: I am not here to sell you a future where software writes itself. I am here because the tools got genuinely useful, and nobody sat me down in a classroom and explained how to actually work with them. So here is that class.

The goal is not to type less. The goal is to spend your thinking on the parts that need a human.

list.text: Used ChatGPT for anything, coding or not.
Used an AI assistant inside an editor (Copilot, Claude, Cursor).
Heard of an agent that edits files and runs commands on its own.
Built something with an ESP32 or Arduino.

note.text: Hands up, or a number in the chat. I will read them out.

slides.title: Chapter 1 — Me, and a website about circuits
slides.subtitle: The unglamorous version of the journey

slides.title: I was a PSGCAS-shaped person too
slides.caption: Dramatisation. The cape is aspirational. The 500 errors are documentary.

box.content: MCA, then a B.Sc. in Computer Science, both in Coimbatore. No dramatic origin story. I liked making things that talked to hardware, so I chased jobs that let me do that.

slides.title: What I actually did for 2.5 years

box.content: The CV says "integrated RFID systems." The reality was closer to this:

list.text: 150+ production issues diagnosed and closed, mostly at hours I would rather forget.
Byte-level UID and CSN conversion — because two readers from two vendors never agree on endianness.
RS-232 timeouts that behaved perfectly in the lab and failed only on site, only on Fridays.
SQL deadlocks under load, offline sync that lost transactions, thermal printers with opinions.

note.text: None of this was in a tutorial. All of it is what the job actually is.

slides.title: The bug that taught me the most
slides.caption: The illustrator guessed Day 14. My actual log said sixteen.

box.content:
A self-checkout kiosk kept marking books as "not returned" for one specific library, and only after 6 PM. Two weeks of logs. The reader was fine. The database was fine. The network was fine.

It was the tag UID. One vendor sent it most-significant byte first, the other least-significant. After 6 PM their staff switched to a spare handheld from the other vendor. The bytes were being compared in opposite order.

The fix was four lines. Finding it was fourteen days. That ratio never really changes — and it is exactly the part AI is worst at.

box.title: circuitdigest.com — published by Semicon Media, Coimbatore

list.text: One of the most-read electronics and embedded systems publications online.
Build guides for Arduino, ESP32, Raspberry Pi, STM32 — real circuits, real code, real photos.
Component explainers, datasheets in plain language, and honest hardware reviews.
Read by students, hobbyists, and working engineers in more countries than I can list.

slides.title: Circuit Digest Cloud — what I build now
slides.imageAlt: Cartoon of a tiny ESP32 chip lifting a barbell of data up to a smiling cloud
slides.caption: An ESP32 has about 320 KB of RAM. This is roughly how the upload feels.
slides.content:
Tutorials are one half. Infrastructure is the other.

Circuit Digest Cloud handles the unglamorous parts of an IoT product:

  • Device provisioning and fleet management for ESP32-class hardware.
  • MQTT telemetry ingestion with live dashboards.
  • Alerts over email, SMS, and WhatsApp when a reading crosses a line.

list.text: FastAPI + PostgreSQL + MQTT for ingestion and device-facing APIs.
GPS tracking with polygon geofencing and live maps.
Computer vision for number-plate, helmet, and object detection, plus live video.
Shipped on DigitalOcean with GitHub Actions and Sentry watching for the 2 AM surprises.

slides.title: How a sensor reading becomes a dashboard

note.text: Every box on this diagram is a final-year project someone in this room could ship.

box.content: Which of your projects is secretly an IoT platform waiting to happen? Attendance systems, lab equipment, hostel water tanks, your bike.

note.text: Say one out loud. I will tell you the three hard parts you have not thought about yet.

slides.question: In that architecture, what is MQTT actually doing?
options: Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging between devices and the backend
slides.explanation: MQTT is a lightweight pub/sub protocol built for flaky networks and tiny devices. The device publishes; a backend service subscribes. Storage and alerting happen downstream.

slides.title: Chapter 2 — From autocomplete to whatever this is
slides.subtitle: A short, opinionated history

list.text: Autocomplete era: it finished your line. Sometimes correctly.
Chat era (2022): you asked, it answered, you copied and pasted and prayed.
Editor copilots: it moved into the IDE and could see your open file.
Agent era (now): it reads the repo, runs the tests, reads the errors, and tries again.

slides.title: The colleague who never sleeps and never brings snacks
slides.imageAlt: A frazzled four-armed robot coding at 2:47 AM surrounded by coffee cups
slides.caption: 2:47 AM. Fourth coffee. "Project: almost done." It is not almost done.
slides.content:
The word that matters is agency

A chatbot can explain a bug to you. An agent can open the file, reproduce the bug, patch it, run the suite, and hand you a diff.

Same underlying model. Completely different thing to work with.

slides.title: A chatbot vs an agent
leftPoints: You copy, paste, wire it up, and verify
Great for learning and getting unstuck
One turn at a time, you drive every step
rightPoints: Reads files, runs commands, edits code directly
Plans, acts, checks the result, corrects itself
Can read docs and confirm its own work
Chases a goal across many steps

note.text: Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex are all in the right-hand column. That is the shift.

list.text: OpenAI — GPT models, ChatGPT, and the Codex coding agent.
Anthropic — the Claude models and the Claude Code CLI.
Google DeepMind — Gemini models and the Antigravity agentic IDE.
Meta — the Llama family, which you can download and run yourself.

box.content:
Most "AI will replace developers" posts are written by people who have never been paged at 3 AM to fix a data migration.

The job was never typing. It is deciding what to build, noticing when the requirements are wrong, and being the person who understands the system when it breaks. AI moves the typing. It does not move the responsibility.

slides.caption: Every AI keynote has this exact chart. Here is ours, for compliance.

box.content:
I could show you a real adoption number. You would forget it by the next slide, so here is the honest version instead.

In 2022, using AI at work was a party trick. In 2026, not using it is the thing that gets a comment in code review. That is the whole trend.

list.text: ChatGPT
GitHub Copilot
Claude
None yet, and that is a completely fine place to start

note.text: A letter in the chat is enough.

slides.question: What is the single biggest difference between a conversational AI and an agentic one?
options: The agent uses a larger model
The agent can take actions in your environment, not just answer
There is no real difference, it is marketing
slides.explanation: Agency (reading, acting, and checking inside your actual environment) is what separates a chat window from a coding agent.

slides.title: The skill that matters now
slides.caption: "Algorithms and Suffering" is not a real book. It should be. Fundamentals still win.

list.text: Prompting — giving enough context and clear constraints.
Verifying — reading output like you would review a stranger's PR.
Knowing the limits — where it hallucinates, where its knowledge is stale.
Security sense — not pasting secrets, not trusting generated auth code blindly.

box.content: We are literally at a university, so, plainly:

list.text: AI is excellent for learning, prototyping, and getting past a stuck point.
Follow your department's actual policy on AI in coursework and research. Ask if it is unclear.
If you cannot explain it in a viva, you do not own it yet. The examiner finds that out in about 40 seconds.

slides.title: Chapter 3 — Using it without making a mess
slides.subtitle: Where it helps, where it lies, and how to ask

list.text: Old: plan, write, test, review, deploy — every step by hand.
New: same steps, but an agent drafts, explains, and tests alongside you, while you stay the one who decides what "correct" means.

slides.title: A loop that does not end in regret
slides.content:
idea / ticket                                          
       |                                                 
       v                                                 
  [ AI drafts a plan ] --> [ YOU review the plan ]       
                                     |                   
                                     v                   
                          [ AI writes the code ]         
                                     |                   
                                     v                   
            [ YOU + AI review the diff ] --> [ tests ]   
                                     |                   
                                     v                   
                               [ deploy ]

note.text: A human checkpoint before the agent acts, and after. That is the entire discipline.

slides.title: Where it genuinely pulls its weight

list.text: Boilerplate and scaffolding — a new component, config, a project skeleton.
Explaining a codebase you were handed an hour ago.
First-draft tests for code that already works.
Debugging when you have a real stack trace to hand it.
Learning a new framework by building something small in it.

slides.title: Where it will confidently lie to you

box.content: It is never unsure. That is the dangerous part.

list.text: Architecture and trade-offs — it will pick one and defend it either way.
Security review — it misses the subtle holes, cheerfully.
Domain judgement — it does not know your users or your rules.
"Is this actually correct" — only you and the tests can answer that.

box.content:
Me: add pagination to the users endpoint

Done. Added limit and offset params, a total count, and updated the docs.

Me: that file you edited is not the users endpoint

You are absolutely right, and I apologise for the confusion. Correcting it now.

Me: also this is FastAPI, not Flask

Of course. My mistake. Here is the version using FastAPI Query parameters.

Me: ok that one actually works

Glad I could help. Would you like me to add tests?

Me: ...yes

note.text: This is the normal experience. It is still faster than doing it alone. You just have to stay in the room.

list.text: Give context: paste the real error and the real file, not a summary of them.
Set constraints: language, framework, style, and what it must not touch.
Iterate: small steps you can check beat one giant prompt you cannot.
Ask for reasoning before you accept a change you do not fully follow.

box.title: Same request, very different afternoon
box.code:
// Vague - invites guessing
"fix my code"

// Specific - grounded in reality
"In src/api/users.py, GET /users/{id} returns 500
when id is not numeric. Traceback below. Add
validation that returns 400 with a clear message,
matching validate_order_id() in src/api/orders.py.
<paste traceback>"

slides.title: Try it: what is your first move?
slides.caption: A codebase you have never seen, on day one. This is the feeling. Ask for the map first.

box.content: You have just cloned a large, unfamiliar repo. What is the very first thing you ask an agent to do?

note.text: Two or three answers, then I will show you what I actually do.

slides.question: Which is the strongest way to ask an AI to fix a bug?
options: The exact file, the exact traceback, and the expected behaviour
slides.explanation: Grounded, specific context turns a guess into a targeted fix. Vague prompts get vague, confident, wrong answers.

slides.title: Before you let it near main

list.text: Read every line. Do not merge what you have not read.
Actually run it. Do not just nod at it.
Grep for keys, tokens, and hardcoded credentials.
Test the edge cases it did not mention.
Be able to explain it — in review, in a viva, in an interview.

note.text: Rule of thumb: if you would be embarrassed to have written it, do not ship it under your name.

slides.title: The human stays in the loop
slides.imageAlt: A team meeting where the whiteboard reads AI DO NOT TOUCH MAIN BRANCH and a cheerful robot says I CAN DO THAT
slides.caption: The whiteboard says do not touch main. The robot says "I can do that." Your job is to stay between them.
slides.content:
Every workflow here has a human checkpoint

That is not overcaution. It is the line between using AI as a tool and quietly outsourcing your judgement to it.

slides.title: Chapter 4 — The actual tools
slides.subtitle: What each one is, and when to reach for it

slides.title: What we will actually look at

list.text: ESP-IDF — the framework ESP32 firmware is built in.
GitHub — repos, CI/CD, and where most AI tools plug in.
Google Antigravity — Google DeepMind's agentic IDE.
OpenAI Codex — OpenAI's cloud and CLI coding agent.
Claude Code — Anthropic's terminal-first agent.

box.title: Espressif's official SDK for ESP32-class chips

list.text: Built on FreeRTOS — real multitasking on a microcontroller.
A component system for reusable drivers and libraries.
idf.py to build and flash, menuconfig for build options.
JTAG and OpenOCD for real debugging, not just serial-print archaeology.

slides.title: Why an embedded framework is in an AI talk
slides.imageAlt: Isometric cartoon of a circuit board drawn as a small town called Microville
slides.caption: Welcome to Microville, population 1024. Every IoT project starts in a town like this.
slides.content:
Because Circuit Digest projects need firmware

Nearly every ESP32 build eventually needs custom code. An agent in your editor can scaffold a FreeRTOS task or wire up a sensor driver while you keep your attention on the actual circuit and the actual timing.

slides.title: GitHub — the boring backbone that runs everything

list.text: Repos and pull requests — where review actually happens.
Actions — the pipeline that deploys Circuit Digest Cloud.
Copilot — inline, autocomplete-style suggestions.
Codespaces — a full dev environment in the browser.
Pages — free static hosting, like the site this deck runs on.

box.title: A coding agent, cloud and CLI

list.text: Runs tasks in a sandbox, on its own.
Hands work back as a reviewable pull request, not a silent overwrite.
Best on well-scoped jobs: "add this endpoint," "fix this failing test."
Also a local CLI for terminal-driven work.

box.title: An agentic IDE from Google DeepMind

list.text: Browser sub-agents that verify UI changes visually.
Produces task and walkthrough artifacts so you can follow what it did.
Deep, whole-codebase context, not just the open file.
There is a full deep-dive deck on Antigravity in this same catalog.
Reads and edits files, and runs your commands directly.
MCP lets it connect to external tools and data sources.
Subagents and hooks for larger, multi-step jobs.
Plan mode proposes a plan for you to approve before it touches anything.

slides.title: Full disclosure
slides.imageAlt: A developer calmly drinking coffee while the room is on fire
slides.caption: Artist's impression of the render pipeline for this deck. It shipped anyway.
slides.content:
This deck was assembled with Claude Code

Working directly in the codebase of the site it runs on. If a slide is ugly, that one is on me, not the model.

list.text: Claude Code — you live in the terminal, want MCP integrations and a review-first flow.
Antigravity — UI-heavy work that needs visual, browser-based checking.
Codex — scoped, PR-sized tasks you can hand off and review later.
Copilot — a light, always-on autocomplete layer next to any of the above.

note.text: You will probably end up with two of them open at once. That is normal.

slides.title: Starting tonight, for real
slides.caption: The sticky-note phase is optional. Start on one small repo instead.

list.text: Install the CLI or extension, sign in with your provider account.
Do not start on something critical. Use a small personal repo.
Give it a task you already know the answer to, so you can judge its work.
Read its plan before you let it run. Every one of these tools supports that.

slides.question: Which tool fits a task that needs a UI change verified visually in a browser?
slides.explanation: Antigravity's browser sub-agents can screenshot and interact with a live page, which is exactly what confirming a UI change needs.

list.text: Pick a small open-source repo you are curious about.
Ask an agent to explain one function you do not understand.
Ask it to write one unit test for that function.
Read the test. Run it. Decide for yourself if it is correct.

note.text: Low stakes, and it teaches the whole review discipline in one sitting.
